key_insight: AI-translated literary texts can be understandable and acceptable, but readers still tend to prefer human translations for literary feel and immersion. The paper shows that “fine” is not the same as “preferred” when quality is judged by real readers.
problem_solved: The paper tackles the gap between standard MT evaluation and the actual reader experience in literary translation. It asks whether AI-generated translations preserve not just meaning and fluency, but also immersion, style, and literary effect.
method: Asked 15 avid readers to compare recently published human translations with machine translations.
Used machine translations produced by an agentic LLM-based translation pipeline.
Focused on reader-centered evaluation, emphasizing immersion and literary effect rather than only adequacy/fluency metrics.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that automatic metrics and traditional human evaluation may miss what matters most in creative language tasks. It suggests that literary translation systems should be optimized and evaluated with reader experience in mind, not just surface correctness.

paper_title: AI translation of literary texts is "fine", but readers still prefer human translations
paper_authors: Yves Ferstler, Adam Podoxin, Ty Brassington, Roman Grundkiewicz, Maite Taboada
